doc.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013

title: Commissions, the BMI workshop and the Air Force Band piece
summary: Whether he prefers guidelines for a commission; the BMI Composer's Workshop and his first commission, a big band piece featuring tenor and bass.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I’ve often wondered about — I do some writing myself, and I wonder sometimes about, let’s suppose I had a decent amount of money to spend, and I was going to commission you to write something. Is it easier for you if you have no guidelines, or if you have some guidelines?

Very good question. I have to say right now I would prefer none. However, that means you have to accept whatever you get. Now generally someone says well this is the ensemble that I want. But they don’t tell you what to write. That’s okay. And I’ve learned to arrange, and that’s different too. But you know, someone gave me a choice, and I have

been involved with this BMI Composer’s Workshop with Manny Albam and Jim McNeeley. Brookmeyer started it but I got a chance to be around all of those guys. And so they’re really composers, I mean serious composers. But Manny was like a composer, but he was really like, we used to call him the “half hour of the incredible arrangers.” He could come up, in a half hour, he would have an arrangement that would just sound great. And that’s a skill, a true skill. But my very — yeah I guess it was my first real commission that came to me not through the BMI program, an Air Force — I wrote something for an Air Force Band in Europe. And he says, “Well I’d like you to write something for the band, and you can either arrange something or you can write something.” And I was right in the middle of the Composer’s Workshop and I said “well I’d better try to write something.” He says, “Well great, but could you write something for a tenor and bass duo, kind of reminiscent of John Coltrane and Paul Chambers.” And it was like okay. I mean he kind of put some handcuffs on.
Right away. But I said okay. I took the challenge with that, and I still came up with something that I still utilize myself now.
Oh, I see, that featured those instruments.

Yeah. He says I have this tenor player in the band and I want to feature him on it and we’ve got a good bass player da, da, da, da. And when he first said that — but, I’m a novice out here. So I was just happy someone was asking me to do anything. So I said, “Well okay, I’ll take that challenge.” And it has turned out, it turned out that he really liked it, and it dovetailed into something else that was totally — I’ve recorded it with my trio, I’ve recorded it — in fact the Air Force Band actually recorded it, flew me down to Texas and we recorded it. So I mean I said “wow — what would have happened if I’d just said no, I don’t want to do that.” So other things — I don’t know. Something told me you’ve got to do this. And it turned out really well.
